PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 39 — Lesson 63: Focused Physical Examination

FNP-level goal: Perform a purposeful, patient-centered physical examination that tests diagnostic hypotheses, identifies instability, documents reproducible findings, and uses normal or abnormal findings appropriately without overclaiming what an examination can exclude.

Learning Objectives

  • Choose a focused versus comprehensive examination based on the presenting problem, risk, and clinical setting.
  • Apply inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation in a deliberate sequence.
  • Use symmetry, comparison, and trends to improve detection of meaningful abnormalities.
  • Protect privacy, obtain consent, use appropriate draping, and adapt the examination to ability, trauma history, and cultural needs.
  • Connect examination findings to physiology, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, and disposition.
  • Recognize when a normal examination does not safely exclude time-sensitive disease.

Part 1 — A Physical Examination Has a Question

A focused examination is not a shortened comprehensive examination. It is a set of maneuvers chosen to answer questions raised by the history, general survey, and vital signs. A patient with acute dyspnea needs assessment of work of breathing, oxygenation context, lungs, heart, perfusion, edema, and possible thromboembolic clues; a patient with dysuria may need a far more targeted assessment. A preventive visit or complex undifferentiated presentation may justify a broader exam.

Before touching the patient, state what you plan to examine, ask permission, offer a chaperone when appropriate, use an interpreter when needed, and ensure comfort, privacy, and draping. The examination is also a therapeutic encounter. Rushed, unexplained, or unnecessarily exposing maneuvers can reduce trust and yield poorer data.

Part 2 — The Four Core Techniques

Inspection begins at the doorway and continues throughout the encounter. Observe appearance, distress, posture, gait, skin color, symmetry, swelling, respiratory effort, mental status, speech, movement, and visible lesions. Inspection is active reasoning: notice what is present, what is asymmetric, and what is changing.

Palpation assesses temperature, tenderness, texture, masses, pulses, edema, expansion, and organ-related findings. Begin gently and watch the patient’s face; palpation can provoke pain and guarding. Percussion uses sound and vibration to estimate underlying air, fluid, or density in selected systems. Auscultation listens for heart, lung, vascular, and abdominal sounds in context. These techniques are not independent rituals: inspection and palpation tell you where and how to listen, and findings should be interpreted together.

Part 3 — Compare Symmetry and Establish a Baseline

Many bedside findings become more useful when compared side to side or with the patient’s prior baseline. Compare breath sounds across matching lung fields, radial pulses, edema, limb circumference when clinically indicated, strength, sensation, pupil reactivity, skin temperature, range of motion, and focal tenderness. Asymmetry often matters more than a vague global impression.

State what you actually found. “Breath sounds diminished at the right base compared with the left” is more useful than “lungs abnormal.” “Pitting edema to the mid-shin bilaterally” is more reproducible than “leg swelling.” Avoid falsely precise grades or labels when you are uncertain; describe the finding, its location, symmetry, timing, and effect on function, then seek supervision or further testing when appropriate.

Part 4 — Cardiorespiratory Examination: Link Finding to Physiology

For a patient with chest or breathing symptoms, examine respiratory rate and effort, ability to speak, accessory-muscle use, oxygenation context, tracheal position when indicated, chest expansion, percussion in selected cases, breath sounds, crackles/wheeze, heart rate/rhythm, murmurs when heard, jugular venous assessment in appropriate settings, pulses, capillary refill, and edema. Auscultate systematically in a quiet environment and compare matching areas.

Interpret findings as clues, not final diagnoses. Crackles can occur with pulmonary edema, pneumonia, interstitial processes, or other conditions. Wheeze may reflect asthma/COPD, heart failure, anaphylaxis, obstruction, or other causes. Reproducible chest-wall tenderness can support a musculoskeletal cause but does not by itself exclude ACS. Severe dyspnea, hypoxemia, cyanosis, altered mentation, hypotension, syncope, new focal neurologic symptoms, or signs of poor perfusion require urgent escalation regardless of an incomplete or initially unrevealing exam.

Part 5 — Abdominal Examination: Sequence Matters

For an abdominal assessment, inspect before auscultation, then percuss and palpate. Palpation can alter bowel sounds and can increase discomfort, so do not begin with deep palpation. Observe distention, scars, visible masses, hernias, bruising, respiratory movement, and the patient’s willingness to move. Auscultate when it addresses the question, then percuss and palpate gradually—beginning away from the most painful location.

Assess localized versus diffuse tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound/peritoneal concern, masses, organ enlargement when feasible, flank tenderness, and signs of volume loss or bleeding. No single maneuver rules in or rules out appendicitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, obstruction, ectopic pregnancy, GI bleeding, ischemia, or other serious pathology. Pregnancy potential, vital signs, medication exposure, prior surgery, and time course are as important as the abdominal examination itself.

Part 6 — Neurologic and Musculoskeletal Screening: Function First

A focused neurologic screen may include level of consciousness, orientation, language, facial symmetry, pupils, extraocular movements when relevant, motor symmetry, pronator drift, sensation, coordination, gait, and targeted reflexes. The selection depends on the complaint. New focal weakness, aphasia, facial droop, visual loss, severe abrupt headache, seizure with persistent altered status, or acute gait inability changes the encounter to emergency evaluation.

Musculoskeletal assessment begins with function: observe gait, ability to transfer, range of motion, joint swelling, erythema, warmth, deformity, focal tenderness, and neurovascular status. Examine above and below an injured area when appropriate. A hot swollen joint with fever, inability to bear weight, trauma with deformity/neurovascular compromise, or back pain with bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, or progressive weakness is not a routine outpatient musculoskeletal problem.

Part 7 — Skin, Peripheral Vascular, and Head-to-Toe Clues

Skin may reveal infection, drug reaction, vascular disease, anemia, jaundice, cyanosis, dehydration, pressure injury, melanoma concern, or systemic illness. Describe morphology and distribution: macule/papule/plaque/vesicle/pustule, color, border, scale, warmth, tenderness, blanching, mucosal involvement, and evolution. Avoid a diagnosis based on a photograph or one descriptor alone when the presentation is high risk.

Peripheral vascular assessment can include temperature, color, pulses, capillary refill in context, edema, varicosities, ulceration, and symmetry. A painful, pale, cool, pulseless, or numb limb may represent acute limb ischemia and needs emergency assessment. Unilateral swelling can have many causes; do not diagnose or exclude DVT from physical findings alone. Use clinical probability and appropriate imaging pathways.

Part 8 — Normal Does Not Always Mean Safe

Physical examination findings have variable sensitivity, specificity, and interobserver reliability. A normal lung examination does not exclude pulmonary embolism; a normal early abdominal examination does not exclude evolving appendicitis; a normal neurologic examination at one moment does not exclude TIA. The meaning of a finding depends on pretest probability, time course, patient risk, and the quality of the examination.

When the history and examination disagree, pause. Re-check vital signs, repeat the exam, seek another examiner, review records, consider targeted testing, and give explicit return precautions. Do not document a reassuring exam as proof that a dangerous alternative has been eliminated when the clinical picture does not support that conclusion.

Part 9 — Documentation and Infection Control

Document the examination you performed, not a template you meant to perform. Include important positives and meaningful negatives linked to the differential, as well as the patient’s tolerance and any limitations. State whether a chaperone, interpreter, or modified technique was used when relevant. Hand hygiene, equipment cleaning, standard precautions, and respectful draping are part of examination quality.

Good documentation allows a future clinician to recognize change. “New unilateral 2+ pitting edema with calf tenderness and tachycardia” supports a different pathway from “chronic symmetric ankle edema unchanged from baseline.” A copied normal exam can conceal deterioration and harms continuity.

Part 10 — Clinical Case: Chest Pain With Reproducible Tenderness

A 61-year-old with diabetes has central chest discomfort after lifting boxes. Palpation reproduces some pain at a costochondral junction, but the patient also reports diaphoresis and worsening discomfort while walking upstairs.

FNP reasoning: reproducible tenderness makes a musculoskeletal contributor plausible; it does not cancel cardiometabolic risk or exertional/associated symptoms. Reassess stability and treat ACS as a consequential alternative requiring the appropriate urgent pathway. Do not use one physical finding to close a dangerous differential.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: The Quiet Patient With Abdominal Pain

A 28-year-old presents with lower abdominal pain, light vaginal bleeding, nausea, and dizziness. The abdomen is only mildly tender, and vital signs are initially near normal.

FNP reasoning: pregnancy status, time course, pelvic symptoms, and dizziness are central. A mild early abdominal exam does not exclude ectopic pregnancy or another time-sensitive process. Obtain appropriate urgent evaluation based on pregnancy test, stability, and local emergency resources.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: New Asymmetry

A patient has sudden unilateral leg swelling, tenderness, and dyspnea after prolonged travel. The leg is warm with intact pulses.

FNP reasoning: intact pulses do not address venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism risk. Create a focused VTE problem representation, assess stability, and follow appropriate urgent diagnostic pathways rather than labeling the finding “cellulitis” or “edema” from inspection alone.

FNP Focused-Examination Framework

  1. Start with consent and safety: privacy, chaperone/interpreter needs, general survey, and emergency red flags.
  2. Let the history choose the exam: use purposeful maneuvers that test the differential.
  3. Use technique deliberately: inspect, palpate, percuss, and auscultate; remember the abdominal sequence.
  4. Compare: side-to-side symmetry, baseline, and trend improve interpretation.
  5. Describe, do not overlabel: location, quality, timing, symmetry, and functional effect.
  6. Integrate findings: physical signs update probability but rarely stand alone.
  7. Escalate and safety-net: instability, high-risk patterns, or discordance require urgent reassessment or emergency evaluation.

High-Yield Summary

Focused exam: selected to answer a clinical question; comprehensive exam is reserved for appropriate settings.
Core methods: inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation are linked techniques.
Symmetry: compare similar areas to identify meaningful differences.
Abdomen: inspect → auscultate → percuss → palpate.
Normal exam: does not independently rule out evolving or high-risk disease.
FNP standard: combine respectful technique, physiology, diagnostic probability, documentation, reassessment, and safe disposition.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Physical-examination technique, diagnostic testing, emergency triage, referral, and treatment decisions must follow current evidence, local policy, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
